caveat: Pectoralis major is commonly described anatomically as clavicular and sternocostal heads, with subdivisions within the sternocostal fibers; it does not have three independently isolatable gym muscles. The planner uses upper, middle, and lower functional fiber regions because exercise angle can shift relative EMG emphasis, while every listed movement still recruits overlapping chest fibers. These entries are content candidates, not training prescriptions.

evidence.supports: Pectoralis major structure, multiple origins converging to one tendon, and differing actions of clavicular versus sternocostal fibers; informs anatomical region labels and the non-isolation caveat.
evidence.title: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Pectoral Muscles (StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf)

evidence.supports: Peer-reviewed EMG study reports greater upper-portion activity at 30° incline and greater middle/lower activity at flat bench; higher inclines shift demand toward anterior deltoid. Supports relative regional bias, not isolation claims.

evidence.supports: Research on common bench-press variations and pectoralis major regional EMG; supports treating press variations as options that may alter relative recruitment rather than isolate a chest subdivision.
evidence.title: Effect of 12 Variations of the Bench Press Exercise on the EMG Activity of the Pectoralis Major (IUSCA Journal)

parts.anatomy_note: The clavicular fibers are the pectoralis major's upper region; shoulder flexion is a function they can contribute to, and a modest incline can bias this region without isolating it.

caveat: Upper back is a practical movement-region label, not one muscle, and its rowing/reverse-fly options involve overlapping scapular retractors, rear deltoids, and other muscles. The trapezius is one continuous muscle with functionally distinct fiber regions, not separately isolatable heads. Lower-back exercises load spinal extensors alongside hip and trunk musculature; no exercise here should be understood as isolating the lower back. Equipment labels reflect common gym setups; assisted pull-up is categorized as machine and bodyweight-only movements as bodyweight.

evidence.supports: Describes latissimus dorsi and erector spinae actions, middle/lower trapezius functions, and reports EMG comparisons for pulldowns, pull-ups, rows, I-Y-T raises, and back extension-related training context. Study findings are limited to its tested exercises and participant sample.
evidence.title: ACE-sponsored research: What Is the Best Back Exercise?

evidence.supports: Exercise-reference index lists back exercise categories and equipment modalities including barbell, cable, dumbbell, lever/machine, and bodyweight options; supports the practicality of the selected exercise patterns.

caveat: The deltoid is commonly organized in workout planners into three broad anatomical regions—anterior, lateral/middle, and posterior—not three perfectly isolated muscles. Research describes finer intramuscular segments, but these are not ordinarily selectable gym-training targets; exercise lists therefore indicate reasonable region emphasis, not exclusive activation. Exercise options are content candidates, not training prescriptions.

evidence.supports: Peer-reviewed anatomical study: establishes the conventional anterior, middle, and posterior portions, their origins, and finer intramuscular segmentation; supports using the conventional three selectable planner regions rather than claiming each is a fully isolated muscle.

evidence.supports: Peer-reviewed exercise study comparing anterior, medial, and posterior deltoid activation in bench press, dumbbell fly, shoulder press, and lateral raise; its limitations caution against treating activation findings as proof of isolation or universal rankings.
evidence.title: Different Shoulder Exercises Affect the Activation of Deltoid Portions in Resistance-Trained Individuals

evidence.supports: Provides a standard dumbbell lateral raise, equipment, beginner difficulty, and practical execution guidance; supports a commonly selectable exercise option.

caveat: Biceps brachii has two anatomical heads, but they merge into one belly and cannot be treated as independently selectable muscles based on ordinary curl variations. This planner therefore lists the whole biceps brachii as one part and the anatomically distinct brachialis as a second part; exercise labels indicate functional emphasis only, not exclusive recruitment. Brachialis can contribute to all elbow-flexion exercises.

evidence.supports: The two scapular heads, common distal muscle belly and insertion, elbow flexion and forearm supination, and limited shoulder actions; supports treating the heads as one overall training target rather than promising head isolation.
evidence.title: Biceps brachii muscle: Origin, insertion, action — Kenhub

evidence.supports: Brachialis location deep to biceps, attachments, and role as a major elbow flexor that works across forearm positions.
evidence.title: Brachialis muscle — Kenhub

evidence.supports: A peer-reviewed EMG study comparing pronated, neutral, and supinated handgrips; reports greater biceps brachii excitation in supinated versus neutral and pronated curls during the lifting phase, supporting grip variation as relative emphasis rather than isolation.

parts.anatomy_note: The long and short heads arise separately from the scapula but unite into one muscle belly and share distal insertion; curls can train the whole muscle, but ordinary gym variations do not reliably isolate either head.

caveat: The three heads are legitimate anatomical parts, but common gym exercises extend the elbow using the triceps collectively; they do not isolate a single head. The categories here are practical selectable emphasis labels, not claims of head-exclusive activation. Overhead shoulder positioning offers a defensible relative long-head bias because it lengthens the biarticular long head; for lateral and medial heads, listed options are standard triceps exercises rather than proven selective isolations. Equipment and levels are content categorization only, not training prescription.

evidence.supports: Three-head anatomy; origins of each head; common olecranon insertion; long head's shoulder crossing and function; medial head participation in forearm extension.
evidence.title: Triceps brachii muscle: Attachments, supply and functions — Kenhub

evidence.supports: Describes an EMG comparison of eight common triceps exercises, electrode recordings on long and lateral heads, and measured activity in triangle push-ups, kickbacks, dips, overhead extensions, pushdowns, lying extensions, and close-grip bench press. Findings support options, not isolated-head claims.
evidence.title: ACE-sponsored Research: Best Triceps Exercises — American Council on Exercise

evidence.supports: Anatomy reference on triceps muscle and head attachments; URL was consulted, but automated text access returned an access-check page, so detailed claims are supported by the readable Kenhub anatomy source instead.
evidence.title: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Triceps Muscle — NCBI Bookshelf

parts.anatomy_note: The long head originates on the scapula and crosses the shoulder as well as the elbow; raising the upper arm overhead lengthens it, but no elbow-extension exercise isolates it.

caveat: The quadriceps has four traditional, anatomically distinct muscles, but standard gym exercises do not practically isolate each one. The eight repeated options are whole-quadriceps candidates for each selectable anatomical label, not claims of selective targeting. A fifth muscle, tensor of vastus intermedius, has also been described, but it is not a practical gym-planner exercise target.

caveat: Hamstrings are a group of distinct muscles, but a gym planner should not present these functional exercise emphases as selectable isolated heads. The first group emphasizes hip extension by loading the hip-crossing long heads; the second emphasizes knee flexion, which can involve all three long hamstrings plus the short head of biceps femoris. Individual activation varies by exercise, technique and person.

evidence.supports: Describes the three hamstring muscles, their locations and shared actions including knee flexion and hip extension; notes biceps femoris is lateral and semitendinosus/semimembranosus are medial.
evidence.title: Hamstring Muscle: What It Is, Anatomy & Function — Cleveland Clinic

evidence.supports: Peer-reviewed EMG study discusses hip-extension-oriented deadlifts and knee-flexion-oriented curls, bridges, Nordic, fitball and slide exercises; reports that some exercises show differential activation but most do not support simple muscle isolation claims.
evidence.title: Muscle and intensity based hamstring exercise classification in professional soccer players

parts.anatomy_note: The semitendinosus, semimembranosus and biceps femoris long head cross the hip and can assist hip extension; these movements train a functional emphasis, not an isolated muscle head.

caveat: The abdominal wall has anatomically distinct muscles, but its oblique layers and deep stabilizers participate in overlapping actions and are not reliably isolated by ordinary gym exercises. Planner categories here are practical functional regions, not claims of muscle isolation. The familiar ‘upper abs’ and ‘lower abs’ are not separate selectable anatomical parts; equipment labels indicate the primary implement rather than exclusive activation.

evidence.supports: Anatomical basis for identifying rectus abdominis and the lateral abdominal muscles, including the external and internal obliques and transversus abdominis, as distinct muscles in an integrated abdominal wall.
evidence.title: Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis: Abdominal Wall - StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf

evidence.supports: Provides common crunch, dead bug, plank, anti-rotation, and other abdominal/core exercise examples; notes that no single exercise trains all abdominal muscles optimally and that abs function integratively rather than only in isolation.
evidence.title: Crunch Time: An Evidence-based Approach to Training the Abs - ACE Fitness

evidence.supports: Reviews EMG research on rectus abdominis, internal/external obliques and transversus abdominis during exercise; reports uneven evidence, measurement inconsistency, and limited transversus-abdominis research, cautioning against overconfident claims of selective targeting.
evidence.title: Core Muscle Activity during Physical Fitness Exercises: A Systematic Review

parts.anatomy_note: The paired rectus abdominis runs vertically on the front of the abdomen and contributes to trunk flexion and abdominal compression; upper/lower ‘abs’ are not separate muscles, though exercise mechanics can shift emphasis.

The internal and external obliques form layered muscles on the sides of the abdominal wall and contribute to trunk rotation, lateral flexion, and bracing; exercises load them together rather than isolating one muscle reliably.
